raw.author: 1Immortals1
raw.text:
not eating for 16 hours to trigger cellular repair sounds like a wellness trend masquerading as science until you read that the 2016 Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded to Yoshinori Ohsumi specifically for his discovery of the mechanisms of autophagy, the process that fasting activates, where your cells literally digest and recycle their own damaged components. then it sounds like the Nobel committee confirmed that not eating activates a repair system so important it won the highest award in medicine

intermittent fasting (typically 16 hours fasted, 8 hours eating) has been practiced in virtually every human civilization. every major religion includes fasting: Ramadan (Islam), Yom Kippur (Judaism), Lent (Christianity), Ekadashi (Hinduism). the religions encoded the practice because the practitioners felt better. modern science explains why: the body switches from growth mode to repair mode when food stops arriving

the mechanism: when you eat, insulin rises and mTOR (the growth pathway) activates. cells grow and divide. when you fast, insulin drops and AMPK (the repair pathway) activates. cells stop growing and start cleaning: damaged proteins are digested, dysfunctional mitochondria are recycled (mitophagy), and misfolded proteins that would otherwise accumulate into disease are cleared. the body can't build AND clean at the same time. eating activates building. fasting activates cleaning. the modern human who eats from 7am to 11pm gives the body zero cleaning hours. the damage accumulates

- the 2016 Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded for the discovery of autophagy mechanisms. the prize committee considered the cellular recycling system activated by fasting important enough to give the highest honor in science
- reduces insulin by 20 to 31% during the fasting window, which sensitizes cells to insulin and reduces the insulin resistance that drives type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and abdominal fat storage
- activates AMPK, the same metabolic master switch that berberine, metformin, and exercise activate. fasting is the oldest and most powerful AMPK activator. it's also free
- increases growth hormone by up to 300 to 500% during the fasting window. the growth hormone increase preserves muscle mass, burns fat, and repairs tissue during the period when food is absent. the body is not cannibalizing muscle during a 16 hour fast. it is protecting it with growth hormone
- reduces inflammation markers (CRP, IL6, TNF alpha) by 20 to 40% in studies of 16:8 intermittent fasting. the inflammation reduction occurs because the NF kB pathway (master inflammatory switch) is suppressed during the fasting window
- brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) increases during fasting, stimulating new neural connections and protecting existing ones. the mental clarity that fasters report by day 3 to 5 is BDNF mediated, not placebo

the diet industry generates $72 billion annually selling food: meal plans, shakes, bars, supplements. fasting sells no food. the industry that profits from you eating cannot promote the intervention that requires you to stop eating. the conflict of interest is structural and permanent. the most effective metabolic intervention available is the one with zero revenue attached to it

start with 14:10 (14 hours fasted, 10 hour eating window) for week 1. progress to 16:8 by week 2 to 3. eat your last meal by 8pm. don't eat until noon the next day. coffee and water during the fast are fine (no calories). the hunger peaks at day 2 to 3 and then decreases permanently as ghrelin (hunger hormone) resets to the new schedule. effects on energy and clarity within 5 to 7 days. body composition changes at 4 to 8 weeks. cost: $0. equipment: a clock

raw.author: DrNikhilMD
raw.text:
🩸 Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM): The Future of Diabetes Care

CGM is one of the most powerful tools in modern diabetology.
It doesn’t just give numbers, it tells the story of a patient’s glucose life in real time.

Unlike HbA1c, which gives a 3-month average, CGM measures interstitial glucose every few minutes, revealing day-to-day fluctuations, nocturnal lows, post-meal spikes, and overall glucose stability.

🔍 Why CGM is Superior to HbA1c in Many Scenarios

HbA1c remains valuable for long-term risk assessment, but it can mislead clinicians in several common conditions.

When CGM is better:
• Anemia, CKD, hemolysis, or recent transfusion – HbA1c is falsely low.
• Iron/B12 deficiency or hypothyroidism – HbA1c is falsely high.
• Pregnancy, steroid therapy, or fluctuating schedules – rapid glucose swings missed by HbA1c.
• Marked variability or hypoglycemia unawareness – same HbA1c, very different risks.

If a patient’s HbA1c looks “perfect” but CGM shows multiple lows or spikes, believe CGM — not the lab.

📊 The 4 Essential CGM Metrics (ADA/EASD Consensus)

✅ Time in Range (TIR) : 70–180 mg/dL → Goal ≥70%
⚠️ Time Below Range (TBR) : <70 mg/dL → Goal <4%
⚡ Time Above Range (TAR) : >180 mg/dL → Goal <25%
📉 Glucose Variability (CV) : Goal <36%

Every 10% rise in TIR ≈ 0.5% reduction in HbA1c — but more importantly, fewer microvascular complications and better quality of life.

🧠 How to Read and Interpret a CGM Report (AGP)

1️⃣ Summary View: Start with TIR, TBR, and CV. this is your control snapshot.
If TBR ≥4%, correct hypoglycemia first before adjusting anything else.

2️⃣ Modal Day Curve: This 14-day overlay highlights patterns.
• Nighttime lows → too much basal insulin
• Early morning highs → dawn phenomenon
• Post-meal peaks → delayed or inadequate bolus

3️⃣ Daily Glucose Traces: Zoom into specific days to identify triggers.
• Weekend highs? → diet or alcohol.
• Day 1 sensor variability? → calibration effect.
• Sporadic drops? → unplanned activity or delayed meals.

💊 CGM-Guided Management Strategies

For Hypoglycemia (TBR ≥4%)
• Stop sulfonylureas if possible.
• Reduce basal insulin by 10–20%.
• If specific lows occur after certain meals, reduce that meal’s bolus by ~10%.
• Persistent daily lows → reduce total daily insulin by 10%.

For Hyperglycemia (TAR ≥25%)
• Rule out missed doses or poor technique.
• Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist (Semaglutide, Tirzepatide) — improves control, reduces weight, and lowers CV risk.
• When adding GLP-1 RA, reduce insulin dose by ~20% if TIR >50% to avoid hypoglycemia.

Always correct technique and behavior before medication:
Check injection site, insulin storage, sensor calibration, and diet timing.

⚖️ Lifestyle & External Influences

• Stress: raises glucose
• Exercise: lowers glucose (watch for delayed lows)
• Alcohol: causes late-night hypoglycemia
• High-dose Vitamin C or Paracetamol: may distort readings in older sensors

🧩 Clinical Pearl

Two patients with the same HbA1c (7%) can have completely different CGM profiles 
One stable, the other with repeated highs and dangerous lows.
Only CGM reveals that difference.

💡 Takeaway

CGM shifts diabetes management from reactive to predictive.
It helps clinicians individualize therapy, prevent emergencies, and empower patients.

HbA1c shows an average.
CGM shows reality.
Always treat the pattern, not the point.

What if we treated high glucose not by giving a drug, but by removing glucose itself?

A study in Science this week describes ECHO, an implantable device designed to do exactly that, without insulin and without medication.

How it works:

The implant sits under the skin and contains an electrocatalyst made of platinum decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in porous graphite.

When wirelessly powered at low power (0.75 volts), the catalyst selectively converts blood glucose into gluconate. Gluconate carries less energy and is cleared by the kidneys into the urine, so both glucose and calories leave the body.

Because the reaction is driven electrically, the rate of glucose removal is adjustable. Turn the current up, remove glucose faster. Turn it off, removal stops.

The closed loop comes from pairing it with a standard continuous glucose monitor. The CGM detects glucose above a set threshold, the implant activates, glucose falls, and the system switches off. In this study it was also smartphone controlled.

What happened in mice with type 2 diabetes and obesity:

Glucose returned to the normal range within 1 hour of activation. Repeated treatment maintained control for 6 weeks with no detectable hypoglycemia. As glucose was removed, metabolism shifted toward fat use. Body weight and triglycerides fell, while free fatty acids and ketone bodies rose. No adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects were detected over those 6 weeks.

This is early stage, mice only, 6 weeks of data. Human questions are unanswered: catalyst durability over years, tissue reaction to a permanent implant, kidney handling of a sustained gluconate load, and whether the glucose removal rate scales from a mouse to a human.

We already have effective human therapies with outcome data, from metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors to GLP-1 receptor agonists and automated insulin delivery. ECHO is not a replacement for any of them today.

It is a proof of concept for a different category: closed loop diabetes care that does not deliver a drug at all, but removes the substrate itself. https://t.co/0DOdZyHWpo

In this article, Prof. Rajesh Khadgawat, Professor, Department of Endocrinology, Metabolism and Diabetes, AIIMS, New Delhi, shares that blood sugar can rise 30 to 90 minutes after eating. A gentle 10-15 minute walk after a meal can help limit this rise. Regular walks of 30-45 minutes in the morning and evening may also support long-term blood sugar control and lower the risk of diabetes and heart disease complications.

If knee pain makes walking difficult, seated or lying-down exercises are a good alternative. If you live with a heart condition, please speak to your doctor before starting any new walk or exercise routine.

#AIIMSNewDelhi #WalkAfterMeals #HealthyLiving #PreventiveHealth #DiabetesAwareness
